predictions.quote: So today, the US has roughly one terawatt of total electricity production capacity... by 2050, the US is projected to build out an additional terawatt to getting us to two terawatts of capacity. So we're going to double our total electricity output by 2050. China, meanwhile, has a plan stated to increase electricity production to 8.7 terawatts, so basically tripling between now and 2050. 88% of their power by 2050 will be renewables. And by 2060 they've stated this goal, that they want about 18% of their overall power to come from nuclear reactors.
predictions.prediction: By 2050, total U.S. electricity generation capacity will approximately double from ~1 TW to ~2 TW. By 2050, China’s electricity generation capacity will increase to about 8.7 TW, with roughly 88% of its power coming from renewables. By 2060, about 18% of China’s total power generation will come from nuclear reactors, if current stated plans are executed.

predictions.quote: They currently have 26 nuclear reactors in the construction phase. They've got planning going on around building 300 of these. and they've already got stated plans, around 500GW of capacity.
predictions.prediction: China will continue its current nuclear buildout, from 26 reactors under construction toward a program targeting roughly 300 reactors and about 500 GW of nuclear capacity over the coming decades (by around mid‑century), consistent with current planning statements.

predictions.quote: Just to give you a sense on the relative cost of electricity, China is about 7 to $0.09 a kilowatt hour. The US is 17 to $0.25 a kilowatt hour, and China is projected to drop their price to less than $0.06 due to the expansion of renewables and nuclear power in the country.
predictions.prediction: As China expands renewables and nuclear power, its average retail electricity price will decline to below $0.06 per kWh in the future (by around 2050), remaining significantly below U.S. retail electricity prices.
